To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the programme had little or no impact, and that we have some evidence to support this conclusion.

(i) in spite of a very small sample size the programme had no appreciable effect on the probability to be in work several months later and that (ii) the instrumental variables approach is a valid tool to test for programme effects in the presence of noncompliance.
the programme had a null effect on the probability to be in work, and that the test for the null hypothesis is powerful enough to be used in practice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the effect of a programme on complying subjects with a score near the selection threshold.
the estimation and testing of the effect of an office automation programme in a regression discontinuous design in which the assignment mechanism does not ensure full compliance.
the estimation and the inference on the effects of a programme in which the treatment is not assigned to all eligible individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the programme did not have a significant impact on the probability of having a job several months after completion, at least for the complying subjects with a score in the neighbourhood of 60.
the programme had a small effect on the probability to be in work, which was not significant.
the office automation training programme had no appreciable effect on the probability to be in work for the complying subjects in the neighbourhood of 40 on the 60-point scale.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a regression discontinuity with imperfect compliance is a useful tool for evaluating training programmes, and that the use of an instrumental variable to account for the contamination of the non-participants is the most appropriate way to identify the effects of such a programme.
the results are not conclusive but the evidence is in the right direction, namely that there is no impact.

the results of the analysis are consistent with the hypothesis that the programme had a negative effect on the probability that complying subjects were in work, but that this effect is small and not significant at the 5 per cent level.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the regression discontinuity design is a useful tool for evaluating training programmes, provided that the researcher is aware of the assumptions that underpin it and that the design can be implemented in a way that makes them plausible.
the instrumental variable estimator is not only a useful tool to identify the causal effect of a programme, but also a useful tool to check whether the programme had any effect at all.
